summary: This bill requires the Comptroller General to create and periodically update a High Risk List for Congress that identifies the program areas and administrative practices posing the greatest risks to Federal funds administered by States and local governments, drawing from existing audits and oversight reports along with best practices and recommendations.

scores.thoughts: The bill directs the Comptroller General to produce a recurring High Risk List focused on program areas and administrative practices that create the greatest risk of waste, fraud, and abuse in federally funded, state-administered programs. It explicitly calls for identifying vulnerabilities, assessing best practices that have already reduced waste/fraud/abuse, and making recommendations to Congress. This is a direct mechanism aimed at improving the integrity and efficiency of existing federal spending rather than authorizing new outlays or expanding programs. Therefore the bill has a moderate positive alignment with reducing government spending.
The bill contains no provisions related to tax rates, tax policy, revenue collection, or any tax expenditures. It is exclusively an oversight and audit measure.
No provisions address healthcare delivery, coverage, funding mechanisms, or regulatory structures in the health sector.
The legislation does not mention firearms, gun regulations, or Second Amendment issues.
No references to immigration policy, border enforcement, visas, or related federal funding streams.
The bill is silent on reproductive health services or abortion access.

While the High Risk List could theoretically encompass any federal program, the bill focuses on state- and locally-administered programs (e.g., pass-through grants subject to single audits). Core national defense functions are not state-administered, so the bill has no meaningful bearing on military spending.
No environmental regulatory, permitting, or climate-related provisions appear in the text.

Many social safety-net programs are state-administered and would fall under the bill’s audit scope, but the legislation neither expands nor contracts benefit levels or eligibility. It only creates an oversight tool to identify waste; therefore it does not push the safety net in either direction.
Education programs are not singled out; the bill is program-agnostic and creates no new education policy or funding rules.
No provisions address controlled substances, enforcement priorities, or decriminalization.
The bill does not alter sentencing, policing, or criminal-justice funding structures.
Trade agreements, tariffs, and import/export policy are outside the scope of this audit-focused legislation.

By highlighting systemic vulnerabilities that lead to waste, fraud, and abuse of federal funds, the bill could indirectly support deficit reduction. The effect is secondary and modest because the legislation itself does not mandate spending cuts or alter appropriations.
No language addresses nondiscrimination protections, gender-identity policies, or related civil-rights matters.
Foreign assistance is administered directly by federal agencies, not through state pass-through programs; the bill therefore has no bearing on foreign aid.
Election administration and voting procedures are untouched by the bill.
Data-privacy rules, technology regulation, and surveillance authorities are not addressed.
The legislation contains no labor, collective-bargaining, or union-related provisions.
No provisions implicate religious exemptions or civil-rights enforcement.
